Agent acceleration

Making LLM agents that operate software finish a task in less time and for less money, without finishing fewer tasks.

Computer-use, web and coding agents, which work a desktop, a browser or a code base one step at a time through a model.

September 2026

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 01
Part 1

Where the time and the money go

Why LLM agents that operate software are slow and expensive, and how the two are linked.

Every number comes from a published measurement of a computer-use, web or coding agent, or from a vendor’s own price page (2024–2026); the conditions of each measurement are stated next to it, and the full references are at the end of the part.

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 02

One attempt of an agent, step by step

here: the loop one attempt runs, and the variable at each step → to: the formulas built from them

One attempt is steps; each step is some model calls plus everything that is not a model call. Every variable below is defined here once; pages 3–4 add them up.

step (one observe–decide–act–wait round); steps in the attempt
model calls in step (planner, judge, retries …); call index
latency of call of step
time to the first generated token: queueing, sending, prefill of the uncached input
output tokens of the call, thinking included; time per output token after the first
model time of step ; all its other time (observe, act, wait, harness gaps, back-off)
time hidden because some of it ran at the same time (AsyncFC’s term, intervals widened); 0 if strictly serial
tokens the result or screenshot of step adds to the prompt of agent
length in tokens of the prompt that step ’s call reads (one call per step); the call’s output as written into that history
input tokens read from the cache, stored in it (a cache write, 5-min or 1-h: ), or uncached
price per token of class on serving model ; billed environment usage (e.g. sandbox hours)
reading = prefill of input tokens; writing = decoding output tokens (a cache write is storage, not output)
probability that one attempt of design on task succeeds

WHAT THE FORMULAS DO NOT SHOW: THE VARIABLES ARE COUPLED
  • The prompt length drives both sides: prefill time and the input bill (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
  • The harness and provider, not the model, set the cache split (Zhu et al., 2026)
  • Time can cost money: a cache entry expires after 5 min or 1 h, so a slow step can turn cache reads into cache writes (our reading of Anthropic, 2026b)
  • Thinking lengthens and the output bill; calls and thinking change (page 13)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 05

Where the time goes: five classes, one per term

from the definition → here: the terms of the time of one attempt, each with one measurement → to: steps and calls

Four of the five are terms of the time equation; the fifth is how they combine: the concurrency term is small in the one production trace that reports it, so the terms nearly add. Which class dominates depends on the harness, not on the kind of agent (page 10). Cause-by-cause tables with measurement conditions: Appendix A1.

I · steps
II · calls per step
III · each call
IV · non-model time
V · little runs concurrently
I · TOO MANY STEPS
Hour-scale tasks take hundreds of steps, and every step is a full round trip
  • 318 tool calls per task on OSWorld 2.0 — 108 desktop tasks, Claude Opus 4.7, one action per step
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
II · TOO MANY CALLS PER STEP
A harness that plans, judges and reflects multiplies every step
  • 4–12 planning calls per judging call — GTA1 harness: four parallel planners, up to three retries, one judge
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
III · EACH CALL IS SLOW
Inside a call, waiting, reading and writing are three separate delays
  • Writing, one token at a time, is 91–98.6% of model time — local 27–31B models with a warm cache
(Yuan et al., 2026)
IV · NON-MODEL TIME
The environment costs time whether or not the model is running
  • 6.6 s per browser action vs 4.7 s per model call, median — 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks, GPT-4o
(Wong et al., 2026)
V · LITTLE RUNS CONCURRENTLY
Almost nothing overlaps, so task time is close to a sum: fixing one term saves only its own share
  • Concurrency within a turn: 1.15 — GitHub Copilot production telemetry
(Liu et al., 2026)
SOURCES · one representative number per class; conditions on pages 6–9 and in Appendix A1

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 06

I–II · Too many steps, too many calls per step

from the five classes → here: the two sums, steps and calls per step → to: what happens inside a call

multiplies every term, and multiplies . Steps accumulate because tasks are long, each step does one action, navigation-only steps still go through the model, and the agent idles or loops; calls accumulate because the harness plans, judges and reflects, or samples several candidates per step.

I-1, I-2 · LONG TASKS, ONE ACTION PER STEP
Long tasks with one action per step need hundreds of steps; several actions per call cut them by half or more
  • 318 tool calls per task with one action per step, 160.7 with several actions per call — OSWorld 2.0, 108 long tasks, Claude Opus 4.7
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
I-3 · NAVIGATION-ONLY STEPS
Most steps are navigation that needs no thinking, yet each one is a model call
  • 66.7% of the steps in the median task are pure navigation — 151 WebVoyager tasks on live websites, three text agents driven by GPT-4o
(Wong et al., 2026)
I-4 · IDLING AND DEAD LOOPS
When an agent is stuck, every repeated step is billed and timed in full
  • One element-locating loop repeated a step 18 times: 27 minutes and $8.47 at list price without caching — GTA1 harness, OSWorld
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
II · PLANNING, JUDGING, SAMPLING
Extra calls per step buy accuracy at a rising token cost per point
  • 10 candidates per step instead of 1: 38.8% → 43.2% success for 96K → 920K tokens per task — gpt-oss-120b, 165 WebArena-Lite tasks
(Lee et al., 2026)
Steps per task on OSWorld 2.0, 108 tasks
XLANG Lab, 2026 · mean over tasks
SOURCES · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Wong et al., 2026 · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026 · Lee et al., 2026 — full rows with conditions in Appendix A1

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 07

III · Inside one call: first token, then decoding

from the two sums → here: the latency of one call, TTFT plus decoding → to: why the prompt keeps growing

A call waits in a queue, reads its uncached input, then writes its output one token at a time: . Queueing depends on the provider, reading on the prompt, writing on how much the model writes, thinking included.

III-1 · QUEUEING
The same request can wait far longer depending on the provider's load
  • Identical requests take up to 69× longer depending on the time of day — 15 models, 5 providers
(Bian et al., 2025)
III-2 · PREFILL
For screenshot agents, reading the prompt dominates a call, and the prompt grows every step
  • Planning, judging and reflection latency is “dominated by the prefill stage” — GTA1 and Agent S2 harnesses, 39 OSWorld tasks
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
III-3 · DECODING
Writing is the slowest segment per token, and thinking modes write far more tokens
  • 224K vs 37K output tokens per task — Claude Opus 4.8 vs GPT-5.5 on the same 108 OSWorld 2.0 tasks
  • Writing is 91–98.6% of model time — local 27–31B models with a warm cache
(XLANG Lab, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026)
HOW TTFT IS MEASURED
Published first-token times lump queueing, network and prefill together
  • Time to first token is measured from the request being sent and “includes network latency”; output speed excludes the first chunk
(Artificial Analysis, 2026)
SOURCES · Bian et al., 2025 · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026 · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Yuan et al., 2026 · Artificial Analysis, 2026 (third-party measurement definitions) — full rows in Appendix A1

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 08

The prompt grows: every step re-reads the whole history

from one call → here: the prompt row of page 3, measured → to: the time outside the model

Each step appends its output and its result, so the tokens read over an attempt grow with ; caching makes re-reading cheaper and faster, not free. The square matters once passes a few dozen steps.

HISTORY RE-SENT
Most computer-use agents send the whole history at every step
  • “At each step, the prompt sent to the LLM includes the history of all previous steps”; later steps take up to 3× longer — GTA1 harness, 39 OSWorld tasks
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
SCREENSHOTS ARE THE BULK
One screenshot adds about a thousand tokens to every later prompt
  • A 1280×720 screenshot is 46 × 26 = 1,196 tokens on Claude, one token per 28×28-pixel patch (calc.)
(Anthropic, 2026b)
CACHED, STILL PAID
A high cache hit rate lowers the price of re-reading, but the prefix stays the larger part of the bill
  • 95.7% hit rate, yet prefix tokens are 59.5% of the list-price cost — 4,265 Claude Code / Codex sessions
(Zhu et al., 2026)
WHEN THE SQUARE BITES
Below a few dozen steps the first prompt dominates; long tasks are deep in the square
  • : a 6,000-token first prompt and 1,500 tokens added per step give (calc., assumed values); OSWorld 2.0 tasks take about 318 steps
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
Per step, the pressure on prefill is the appended part, not the whole prompt: with a warm cache, “the relevant per-turn prefill pressure is better captured by incremental appends” (Yuan et al., 2026).
SOURCES · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026 · Anthropic, 2026b · Zhu et al., 2026 · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Yuan et al., 2026 — the growth rows with conditions are in Appendix A3

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 09

IV–V · The time outside the model, and how little of it overlaps

from the prompt → here: non-model time and concurrency → to: which term dominates

The environment is slow, and today's agents run almost everything in sequence, so is small and the attempt time is close to the full sum. Published “total times” differ in what they count, so the boundary has to be stated.

IV · NON-MODEL TIME
The environment is slow on its own, and the benchmarks add fixed sleeps on top
  • OSWorld 2.0 sleeps 3 s after every action: × 318 steps ≈ 16 min of pure waiting per task (calc.)
  • 6.6 s per browser action vs 4.7 s per model call, median — 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks, GPT-4o
(XLANG Lab, 2026; xlang-ai, 2026; Wong et al., 2026)
V · CONCURRENCY
Almost nothing overlaps, so fixing one term saves only its own share
  • Concurrency within a turn: 1.15 — GitHub Copilot production telemetry
(Liu et al., 2026)
Where a Claude Code / Codex request’s 4.3 minutes go
Zhu et al., 2026 · 4,265 sessions, 43 developers
WHAT A “TOTAL TIME” COUNTS
Some published times include the person, others exclude them
  • 80–92% of a coding session’s elapsed time is the person thinking between turns, outside any one attempt
(Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)
SOURCES · XLANG Lab, 2026 · xlang-ai, 2026 · Wong et al., 2026 · Liu et al., 2026 · Zhu et al., 2026 — full rows in Appendix A1

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 10

Which term dominates depends on the harness, not on the kind of agent

from the five terms → here: their shares, per kind of agent → to: where the money goes

All five classes exist in every agent; the heaviest term differs, and it flips when the harness changes.

Screenshot desktop agent, multi-call harnessText web agentCoding agent with a prompt cache
heaviest Reading × calls per step × steps. 87–97% of task time is planning, judging and reflection calls (GTA1, Agent S2; 39 OSWorld tasks) (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026) Browser execution and waiting. Per step, median: browser 6.6 s, model 4.7 s (151 WebVoyager live-site tasks, GPT-4o) (Wong et al., 2026) Writing, or tool tails. Writing is 91–98.6% of model time (Yuan et al., 2026); in Claude Code / Codex requests tools take 59.8%, the model 41.0% (Zhu et al., 2026)
flips when The harness makes one call per step: over 70% of the time is then the sandbox, because the benchmark sleeps 2–3 s after every action (Chang et al., 2026; xlang-ai, 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026) The observation grows: 4.8× the input moved the model’s share of step time from 46.9% to 61.6% (Chang et al., 2026) Load evicts the cache: latency up to 7.14× (Kang et al., 2026)
in one line Slow in reading: every step re-reads the growing screenshot history Slow in the environment — until the observation grows, then slow in reading Reading is cached away; slow in writing and in the tools
1 · The harness sets the dominant term — calls per step, observation size, fixed sleeps, cache on or off. The explanation “agents are slow because inference is slow” is accurate only for multi-call screenshot agents.
2 · multiplies every term — one step fewer saves a whole step of time and money in all three kinds.

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 11

Where the money goes: six classes, one per term

from where the time goes → here: the terms of money per success, each with one measurement → to: per attempt vs per success

Money comes from tokens read and tokens written, each times a price, plus billed environment usage, which is usually small. Writing costs 5× reading; a cached read costs a small fraction of a normal read (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: $0.006 vs $0.30 per million tokens); fast mode costs 2× (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026; DeepSeek, 2026).

3 · number of calls
1, 2 · tokens by class
5 · price per class
6 · environment
4 · failures, retries
1 · TOKENS READ
Reading is the larger bill and grows with the square of the steps
  • Even at a 95.7% cache hit rate, prefix tokens are still 59.5% of the bill — 4,265 Claude Code / Codex sessions
(Zhu et al., 2026)
2 · TOKENS WRITTEN
Writing is the dearer token, thinking included, but the smaller bill
  • 31% of an uncached screenshot agent’s bill: $2.43 counting output only vs $7.87 counting all tokens — GTA1, 39 OSWorld tasks (calc.)
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
3 · NUMBER OF CALLS
The calls that make the agent slow also make it expensive
  • 5–13× the calls of a single-call harness per step — GTA1: planners, retries and a judge (calc.)
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
4 · FAILURES AND RETRIES
Failed attempts are billed in full
  • $72.4 per attempt ÷ 20.6% completion ≈ $351 per success — OSWorld 2.0, best agent (calc.)
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
5 · UNIT PRICE
The price list sets the constant; fast tiers double it
  • Claude Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 vs GPT-6 Luna $0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens read / written — a 40× spread (calc.)
(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)
6 · THE ENVIRONMENT MACHINE
Published costs are API bills only; a CPU environment adds little
  • $0.02–0.36 for a one-hour CPU environment: 0.3–4.6% of a $7.87 bill (calc.; next page)
vendor price pages, read 2026-09-27

Four accounting conventions for one task, and the cost of the environment machine

from the six classes → here: per attempt vs per success, which convention a figure uses, and the environment → to: how time and money are linked

The same run’s cost differs by up to 30× across the four conventions in use, and none includes the environment machine.

conventionthe same run, counted both waysgap
output only vs all tokensGTA1 on 39 OSWorld tasks, o3 list price, no cache: $2.43 counting output only; $7.87 counting all tokens (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)3.2×
per attempt vs per successOSWorld 2.0, Claude Opus 4.8: $72.4 per attempt at 20.6% completion → ≈ $351 (calc.; a benchmark average) (XLANG Lab, 2026)4.9×
uncached vs cachedA cached read costs a fraction of a normal read (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: $0.006 vs $0.30 per million tokens; other vendors in A3) (DeepSeek, 2026)4–50× on the read price only, by vendor (calc.)
standard vs fast modeClaude Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 → $8 / $40; OpenAI 2× on every listed model; up to 2.5× faster writing (vendor-stated), reading unchanged (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)2×
The three that apply to a whole bill compound to about 31× (3.2 × 4.9 × 2, calc.). Screenshot-agent measurements do not report their cache state.
6 · THE ENVIRONMENT MACHINE, FROM LIST PRICES
For CPU environments the machine is a small addition; idle time, proxy traffic and GPUs change that
  • An H100 sandbox at $3.95 per hour is already half of a $7.87 bill, and hourly billing runs while the agent waits — the median AgentSysBench session is active only 20% of its lifetime
vendor price pages, read 2026-09-27; Chang et al., 2026

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 13

How slow and expensive are linked: three kinds of relationship

from the two sides → here: what each term does to time and to money → to: the levers

Time and money share the token counts; queueing and environment time reach money only through billed environment usage — and through the cache, which expires while the agent waits.

time
money
in both — same sourcetime only, or money only through billed environment usagethe price — money for speed or accuracy
the queueing and prefill parts of (our split; network and first-token time left out; Appendix A0)
one attempt each; divide by for per success
SAME SOURCE — in both equations
fix it, and time and money fall together
  • Steps , calls per step , reading, writing, cache hits, failures — every one of them lives in the token counts
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b)
SLOW BUT NOT EXPENSIVE — no tokens, only machine hours
fix it, and only time falls
  • Queueing, page loads, fixed sleeps, tool tails — none produces a token; the machine behind them is billed by the hour, usually under 5% of the API bill
MONEY FOR TIME OR FOR ACCURACY — opposite signs
paying for speed shortens only the writing segment; paying for accuracy costs more tokens per point as accuracy rises
  • Fast mode: up to 2.5× faster writing (vendor-stated) at 2× the price, reading unchanged
(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026; accuracy: Appendix A4)
TIME THAT COSTS MONEY — the cache expires
a slow step or a long pause can turn cheap cache reads into cache writes
  • A cache entry lives 5 minutes or 1 hour from the start of the last request that read or wrote it; at most 12.8% of cost could be saved if the cache survived human pauses
(Anthropic, 2026b; Zhu et al., 2026)
SOURCES · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026 · Anthropic, 2026b · OpenAI, 2026 · Zhu et al., 2026 — the cause-by-cause table, with the convexity evidence, is Appendix A4

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 14

The levers, and what is still unmeasured

from how time and money are linked → here: what fixing each lever buys, and the holes in the evidence → to: Part 2, what the literature has done with each lever

Seven levers follow from the formulas; each moves one term and carries a known risk. Part 2 asks how far the literature has pushed each. Right: gaps in the evidence, not claims of a research gap.

levertimemoneythe catch
Fewer steps — several actions per call, skip navigation-only stepsyesyes, the quadratic termwhich steps need no thinking?
Read less — trim history, shrink screenshots, cache the prefixyesyesforgets; trimming invalidates the cache
Write less — less thinking, smaller modelyesyesaccuracy may fall
Fewer calls per step — drop judging and reflectionyesyesfewer errors caught
Overlap the waiting — pre-load, parallel tools, page-ready eventsyesnoonly where the environment dominates
Buy a fast or priority tier writing onlyno — 2× morereading unchanged; cache dropped
Stop retrying failures — early stop, detect dead loopsyesyesstops some attempts that would have succeeded
NOT YET MEASURED
  • Read / write time split and cache hit rate for a frontier API model — the only split is on local 27–31B models (Yuan et al., 2026); screenshot-agent measurements do not report cache state.
  • How much slower than a person — no benchmark times agent and human on the same tasks; the closest, AXIS’s small user study, has a UI agent 1.69× slower than manual work on easy tasks (Lu et al., 2025).
  • Whether the benchmark’s fixed sleep sits inside “action” time in OSWorld-Human — if so, “environment under 3.5%” understates the waiting.
  • How much slowness costs accuracy — OSWorld 2.0 records the stale-screen failure mode without its share (XLANG Lab, 2026).
SOURCES · levers derived from the formulas on pages 3–4 · gaps: Yuan et al., 2026 · Lu et al., 2025 · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Appendix A4 and A5

A1 · Slowness, every cause — I. steps and II. calls per step

the complete table behind pages 5–6 · three kinds of agent: screenshot desktop agent, text web agent, coding agent with a prompt cache
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsourcedominant in
I-1The task is longHour-scale tasks take hundreds of stepsOSWorld 2.0, 108 long tasks: Claude Opus 4.7 with maximum thinking, one action per step, 500-step cap: 318 tool calls per task on average, i.e. 318 steps; with several actions per call, Claude Opus 4.8 takes 103 steps (481.8 calls) and GPT-5.5 95.2 steps (149.8 calls)(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot, text
I-2One action per stepEvery click is a whole step: one observation, one model call, one waitOSWorld 2.0: with one action per step Claude Opus 4.7 needs 318 steps; with batched actions the same model needs 160.7 and Claude Opus 4.8 needs 103(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot, text
I-3Navigation-only steps still call the modelPaging, scrolling and opening the next page need no thinking but cost a call eachSkim’s profile of three text web agents (Browser-Use, AgentOccam, WebVoyager; GPT-4o) on 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks: 66.7% of the steps in the median task are pure navigation(Wong et al., 2026)text
I-4Idling and dead loopsElement not found, repeated retries; steps rise without progressOSWorld-Human’s records of the GTA1 harness (o3 plans and judges, GTA1-7B locates elements) on 39 OSWorld desktop tasks: in failed tasks that exceeded 50 steps, 66% of steps were wasted repeats; one element-locating loop repeated the same step 18 times — 27 minutes and $8.47 at list price without caching(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)screenshot
I-5Acting on a stale screenThe screenshot is taken before the page changes; the agent clicks on the old layout and must repairOSWorld 2.0 records “stale interface state” as a failure mode; no share reported(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot
II-1Multi-call harnessOne step = plan + judge + reflect, several calls in seriesOSWorld-Human, two harnesses: GTA1 runs 4 parallel planners per step, retries up to 3 rounds, then one judging call picks — 4–12 planning calls per judging call; Agent S2 adds a reflection call per step, so planning is 53% and reflection 34% of task time(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)screenshot
II-2Sampling for accuracy5–20 candidates per step, then pick oneSame model and harness (gpt-oss-120b, ReAct) on 165 WebArena-Lite tasks: 1 → 10 candidates per step raises success from 38.8% to 43.2% and tokens per task from 96K to 920K — 9.6× the tokens for 4.4 points(Lee et al., 2026)text
II-3Coding agents call repeatedly within a turnThe model is called back and forth inside one user turnGitHub Copilot coding agent production telemetry (first week of June 2026, 13.5 million sessions): 6.6 model calls per user turn on average(Liu et al., 2026)coding

IV-4Tool tailsTests and builds take minutesTraceLab, 4,265 Claude Code / Codex sessions from 43 developers (September 2025 – June 2026): tool calls over 1 minute are 4% of calls but 85% of tool time; a request averages 4.3 minutes — tools 2.5 (59.8%), model 1.7 (41.0%)(Zhu et al., 2026)coding
VSerial structureThe four stages never overlap, so task time is the sum of every term, not the largest one; fixing one term saves only its shareConcurrency within a turn is 1.15 in Copilot telemetry. Separately, 80–92% of a coding session’s elapsed time is the human thinking between turns — strip it before reading any total(Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)all

the complete table behind page 10
screenshot desktop agent, multi-call harnesstext web agentcoding agent with a prompt cache
heaviest termReading × calls per step × steps. OSWorld-Human timed two multi-call harnesses (GTA1, Agent S2) step by step on 39 OSWorld desktop tasks: 87–97% of task time in planning, judging and reflection calls; screenshots and actions together under 3.5% (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)Browser execution plus waiting. With the context cache on, token-by-token generation is 91–98.6% of model time (locally served models) (Yuan et al., 2026); in Claude Code / Codex records a request spends 59.8% in tools and 41.0% in the model (Zhu et al., 2026); in GitHub Copilot, whose tools are light, agent time is 13.7% model and 2% tools (Liu et al., 2026)
secondWriting: with thinking on, more reasoning tokens per step, and generation is one token at a timeReading, once the observation grows: AgentSysBench switched a WebArena agent from one observation format to accessibility tree + HTML + screenshot — input 4.8×, model share 46.9% → 61.6% (Chang et al., 2026); the Browser-Use harness spends 73% of its latency in model calls (Winston et al., 2026)Reading, when load evicts the cache and the whole context is re-read: ThunderAgent measured request latency up to 7.14× under cache thrash (Kang et al., 2026)
negligibleProducing the observation and executing the action: under 3.5% together (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)Nothing: model and browser are close; which is larger depends on observation size and model speedNavigation-only steps: a coding agent has no pages to turn
counter-exampleA single-call agent is different: AgentSysBench’s one-call GUI agent (Kimi-K2.6) spends over 70% of its OSWorld time in the desktop sandbox (Chang et al., 2026), because the harness sleeps after every action — 2 s in OSWorld’s code (xlang-ai, 2026), 3 s in OSWorld 2.0 (XLANG Lab, 2026)Browser-Use: 73% of latency in model calls, not the browser (Winston et al., 2026)Two production records point opposite ways: heavy tools in Claude Code / Codex (tools 59.8% > model 41.0%) (Zhu et al., 2026); light tools in Copilot (model 13.7% > tools 2%) (Liu et al., 2026). The difference is the kind of tool (tests and builds vs file reads), not a contradiction
in one lineSlow in reading: every step re-reads the screenshot history, more as the task goes onSlow in the environment (browser and page waits); once the observation grows, slow in reading againReading is cached away; slow in writing and in the tools

The four accounting conventions (page 12), in one line each: output only vs all tokens — 3.2× (OSWorld-Human, $2.43 vs $7.87); per attempt vs per success — 4.9× (OSWorld 2.0, $72.4 ÷ 20.6%); uncached vs cached — 4–50× on the read price by vendor (calc.), far less on the bill (TraceLab: 95.7% hits, prefix still 59.5% of cost); standard vs fast mode — 2× (both vendors), buying only writing speed.

Many steps Roughly linear: one more step is one more call and one more wait (later steps somewhat slower, up to 3×)Write tokens linear in ; read tokens quadratic, because every step re-reads the whole historysame source — double the steps: about 2× the time, about 4× the read bill (uncached)
Many calls per step linearlinearsame source
Reading a lot (history, screenshots, rich observations)Reading time, longer every stepRead-token billsame source — the same tokens cost time and money
Writing a lot (thinking)Generation time, roughly 12 ms per tokenWrite-token bill at 5× the read pricesame source, and the dearest time: writing is the slowest and the most expensive token
Cache hitsSaves reading timeRead price 0.02–0.25× of a normal read, by vendor (A3)same source, but fragile: editing the history or switching to fast mode invalidates it
Queueingslowfreeslow but not expensive; escaping it means a fast or priority tier at 2×
Environment waits (page loads, fixed sleeps)slowNo API cost; machine time by the hour — CPU sandboxes $0.02–0.36 per hour, usually under 5% of the API billslow but not expensive
Tool tails (tests, builds)slowNo API costslow but not expensive
Failures, idling, retriesslowexpensivesame source, and it turns “per attempt” into “per success”
Fast modeWriting up to 2.5× faster (vendor-stated); reading unchanged2× the pricemoney for time
Bigger models, more thinkingslowerdearermoney and time for accuracy, convex: marginal tokens per point 101K → 575K on one model; 6× / 9× / 9.6× tokens for a few points; more thinking not always more accurate (Lee et al., 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2026)
Smaller modelsfastercheaperbut if accuracy falls, steps and retries rise — possibly slower and dearer again (inference, no direct evidence)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · A5

A5 · The gaps in the evidence, and what each one blocks

the complete table behind page 14
gapwhat exists todayconsequence for what can be claimed
Read / write time split and cache hit rate for a frontier API modelNo measurement reports both; the only read / write split is on locally served 27–31B models (Yuan et al., 2026); screenshot-agent measurements do not report cache stateHow much of “87–97% in the model” is reading, how much writing, and what remains once the cache is on — unknown
How much slower an agent is than a personNone of 17 benchmarks measures agent and human elapsed time on the same tasks; the closest is AXIS’s user study, in which a UI agent was 1.69× slower than manual work on easy tasks (small sample) (Lu et al., 2025)“X times slower than a person” cannot go on a slide
Environment dollarsBenchmarks report instance types; AgentSysBench reports shares; products publish nothing. Computable from instance type × duration × list price: CPU environments usually 0.3–5% of the API bill (page 12)Every benchmark cost is an API bill; the omission is small for CPU environments, not for GPU sandboxes or long idle sessions
Whether OSWorld-Human’s “action” includes the 2-s sleep after each stepNot stated (xlang-ai, 2026); if it does, “actions under 2%” implies more than 100 s per step (calc.)“Environment under 3.5%” may understate the waiting
The rebound from a smaller modelNo direct evidence on how many extra steps and retries a drop in accuracy causesThe last row of the relationship table stays marked “inference”
How much slowness hurts accuracyOnly OSWorld 2.0 records the stale-state failure mode, without its share of failures (XLANG Lab, 2026)“It exists” can be said; “how large” cannot
